headlines.article_text: DNI chief Jay Clayton warns of 'bumps in the road' after tech outages Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said modernization and cybersecurity investment may bring temporary interruptions as systems are upgraded. Recent FAA, Microsoft and JPMorgan disruptions had different root causes, and officials say they do not appear to be part of a coordinated cyberattack. Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testifies during a House Committee on Homeland Security hearing in the Canon House Office Building on Capitol Hill on November 18, 2026 in Washington, DC. Chip Somodevilla | Getty Images Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Americans to prepare for "bumps in the road" after a set of damaging technology outages rocked air travel and systems like Microsoft Outlook. Government officials have largely dismissed the prospects that the outages, which also slowed bank transactions , are linked to a coordinated or artificial intelligence cyberattack. Clayton, however, said on CNN's "State of the Union" that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI age. "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing "You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," he said. Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. A technology outage prompted a nationwide ground stop just over a week ago, which lasted for hours. The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades caused a flood of data that led to the ground stop, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack. Separately, Microsoft said the Outlook outage was caused by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message on CBS' "Face the Nation." Asked if Americans should be concerned about the security of their financial institutions, Bessent said: "No, they shouldn't." "The patches may cause a glitch," he said, referring to measures banks are taking to safeguard from AI. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency." headlines.article_text: Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but he lives on minimum wage Skip Navigation This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money. At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage. For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states. He does it by living with roommates in Washington, D.C., walking or biking instead of driving, eating free meals at work and rarely spending beyond his basic needs. Even when he splurges on something fun, he keeps things modest; in August, that meant a baseball game and a single $7 beer. "I guess something else that probably does make me a little bit unique is I really don't feel joy when I buy things," he says. "I feel like I have what I need." Charles Broomfield in Washington, D.C. Matthew Ritenour | CNBC Make It There is a goal behind all that saving. Broomfield has pursued financial independence since college and now expects to reach his target of $750,000 in investments within the next year, well ahead of his original goal of doing so by age 30. As his income has climbed, his lifestyle has largely stayed the same, he says. Here's how Broomfield keeps his spending so low and what he plans to do once he no longer needs the paycheck. Saving for financial freedom Broomfield grew up in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the son of two military veterans. He and his siblings had to set aside half of everything they earned growing up. They could spend the other half or earn interest from their parents by putting that money away, too. By his teenage years, Broomfield had become a disciplined saver. At the time, he dreamed of using his cash stash to buy some of the familiar trappings of wealth. "I wanted a Lamborghini and I wanted some nice penthouse," he says. "I just wanted them because I thought other people wanted them." At 17, Broomfield discovered Mr. Money Mustache, a personal finance blog by a former software engineer who retired at 30. The blog advocates living frugally and investing much of your income to build a portfolio large enough to support you through withdrawals, without needing a paycheck. It introduced Broomfield to the financial independence, retire early — or FIRE — movement and gave all that saving a new purpose. Charles Broomfield in his bedroom in a Washington, D.C., apartment he shares with four roommates. Matthew Ritenour | CNBC Make It "All I had to do was live super frugally and I could actually reach financial freedom by the time I was 30 and go do whatever actually made me happy in life," he says. The idea stuck with him. After graduating from Knox College in 2022, Broomfield moved to Northern Virginia for a job paying more than $100,000 a year and set a goal of reaching $750,000 in investments before 30 while spending less than $25,000 a year. He also decided to start at $0. Broomfield had roughly $50,000 in savings when he graduated, with his parents having covered the portion of his college tuition not paid for by scholarships. He wanted his FIRE total to reflect only what he earned after college. 'Geeked out' on extreme frugality In his first year after college, Broomfield was "super geeked out" about reaching financial freedom, he says. "It's almost the only thing I thought about, because I was building all these new habits and making real money for really the first time in my life," he says. That enthusiasm sometimes took him to extremes. He even considered living in a van parked in his employer's garage to avoid paying rent. "I crunched the numbers on it, and effectively every year that I spent living in a van rather than paying rent would allow me to retire approximately one month faster," he says. "It just [didn't] seem really worth it to go to that extreme." Charles Broomfield at the grocery store. Matthew Ritenour | CNBC Make It But Broomfield still found satisfaction in squeezing every dollar out of his budget. He once biked two miles to a grocery store to save $1 on toothpaste rather than buy it at the Whole Foods next to his apartment. "For a lot of people, they feel their wins by buying stuff for themselves," Broomfield says. "I get my wins by seeing how much I can invest." Looking back, Broomfield acknowledges that some of his early efforts to save money made little difference in how quickly he could reach financial independence. "I never expect anybody else to do exactly what I'm doing," he says. "I know I'm way more of a geek about this than most people, and I'm particularly well positioned to be able to live this kind of life." How he lives on less than $20,000 a year Broomfield's core living expenses totaled $1,477 in August, excluding savings, investments and payments toward his graduate school tuition. Here's a breakdown of where his money went that month, including those additional payments: Christina Locopo | CNBC Make It Savings and investments: $17,931 in 401(k) and brokerage account contributions. Rent and utilities: $1,098 including electricity, gas and water. Student debt repayment: $700 Gym membership: $229 Discretionary: $59 Transportation: $48 for Uber rides Food: $28 spent on groceries or eating out Insurance: $15 for dental, renters Roughly 90% of Broomfield's income went to savings and investments in August, a fairly typical month for him, he says. He put about $7,931 into his 401(k) and another $10,000 into a taxable brokerage account. Another $700 went toward a 0% interest employer tuition repayment plan with a former employer, leaving him with a remaining balance of $16,800 in August. Housing is Broomfield's biggest expense, though he keeps costs down by sharing an apartment with four roommates. In a neighborhood where one-bedroom apartments commonly rent for more than $2,000, the arrangement saves him about $1,000 a month. One thing Broomfield is willing to splurge on is a martial arts gym membership. He pays $229 a month to train as a kickboxer, even though he could work out for free at Google's office gym. Broomfield considers it a "young person's sport" and doesn't want to postpone competing until after he reaches financial independence. It's also a way to socialize with other amateur fighters who share his interest. Charles Broomfield at the gym where he trains in kickboxing. Matthew Ritenour | CNBC Make It Broomfield doesn't own a car and generally walks, bikes or takes public transportation. Google covers his daily Metro commute, which helps keep his transportation costs low. He tries to meet friends near Metro stations and, when visiting his grandfather in Virginia, takes public transit as far as he can before using Uber for the last leg of the trip. Before joining Google, Broomfield typically spent around $200 a month on food. Now that he eats most of his meals at work , he spends about $70 a month on average. His $28 food bill in August was especially low because he had ingredients left over from July. He also cooks less at home these days. Previously, he relied more on batch cooking, including pressure cooker chili that makes nine servings for about $2 each. For snacks, he might have a bowl of Raisin Bran or celery with peanut butter. “I did the math once, and peanut butter was the lowest cost thing per gram of protein in the entire grocery store,” he says in a video on his YouTube channel, which he started in 2023 to document his FIRE journey. For entertainment, he relies on the free version of YouTube, where he watches educational content about startups, business and entrepreneurship, or listens to music. headlines.summary: Domino's, Papa Johns and Pizza Hut face weaker demand, more delivery competition and changing eating habits, including GLP-1 use.
headlines.article_text: Why Domino's, Pizza Hut and Papa Johns are struggling Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Big pizza chains such as Domino's, Papa Johns and Pizza Hut are under pressure as value-conscious diners choose from more delivery choices and changing eating habits reshape demand. Thousands of U.S. pizza locations have permanently shuttered since the category's peak in 2019. Weaker consumer spending, more dining options and GLP-1 medications have weighed on pizza demand. In this article DPZ PZZA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:25 06:25 Why big pizza chains are struggling CNBC Digital Original Video Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales. The pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza , Papa Johns , Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers. These days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more important to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants. A Papa John's International Inc. pepperoni pizza arranged in Louisville, Kentucky, U.S., on Monday, Feb. 22, 2021. Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty Images As a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential. In 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%. Papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%. It isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period. A worker takes a pizza out of a pan at a Domino's restaurant in Trenton, Michigan, US, on Wednesday, April, 10, 2024. Domino's Pizza Inc. is scheduled to release earnings figures on April 29. Photographer: Nic Antaya/Bloomberg via Getty Images Nic Antaya | Bloomberg | Getty Images And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales. "Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September. Pizza's challenges Pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders. As pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication. Plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data. "When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," said David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana. Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point. "We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June. She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut. The biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day. Pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years. Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC. To be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin said. And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's launched the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a new turnaround plan focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal. "Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin said. "The American consumer loves pizza."
